Nathanael Greene. The commander of the Continental Army's southern department and one of the war's most brilliant strategists. Though he won few pitched battles, he executed a masterful campaign of harassment and supply disruption that exhausted British forces in the Carolinas and Georgia, forcing them back toward the coast.

Greene took command of the southern theater in 1780 after the American collapse at Charleston, inheriting a war of attrition. He divided his small force into mobile units that avoided decisive engagement while attacking British supply lines and isolated garrisons.

He won a strategic victory at Guilford Courthouse in March of 1781 by fighting and retreating in good order, inflicting so many British casualties that General Cornwallis was forced to withdraw toward the coast. Greene deliberately sacrificed the Catawba and Pee Dee river regions, trading space for time to gather supplies and recruits while the British army grew weaker.

He reclaimed Charleston and Savannah by siege and maneuver without major battles, demonstrating that control of territory lay not in one decisive clash but in grinding British supply chains to a halt. Never defeated in the field despite being outnumbered, his attrition strategy proved the template for asymmetric warfare. George Washington gave him operational freedom despite political pressure to fight, and his southern campaign shifted the war's balance in the Patriots' favor.
